new.title: Direct inference of cosmological mass growth via timing of black hole - pulsar binaries
new.summary: Cosmologically coupled black holes (CCBHs) respond to the expansion of the Universe, independently of conventional astrophysical processes. Recent CCBH solutions in General Relativity demonstrate evolution of gravitating mass $m_{\rm BH}\propto a^\kappa$, where $a$ is the cosmological scale factor. This can be tested through the orbital period timing of black hole (BH) pulsar (PSR) binaries. In contrast to previous methods used to constrain $\kappa$, pulsar timing measurement baselines span decades instead of gigayears, allowing sources of bias to be well-controlled. As a test case, we analyze the globular cluster BH+PSR candidate J0514--4002E (spin $P\sim 5.6~{\rm ms}$, orbital period $P_{\rm b}\sim 7~\rm days$) under the assumption that the companion is a CCBH. Taking the difference between the observed orbital and spin period derivatives removes all kinematic effects, leaving only the pulsar's intrinsic spin-down $\dot{P}_{\rm int}$ as unknown. Setting $\dot{P}_{\rm int} = 0$, its physical minimum, gives a robust upper bound $\kappa \leqslant 3.95$ at $95\%$ confidence. We estimate $\dot{P}_{\rm int}$ through the population of millisecond pulsars matched in spin and infer $\kappa = 0.82 \pm 1.67$ and $0.75 \pm 1.54$, using $H_0 = 67.6$ and $73.5\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, respectively. Adopting typical baseline scaling of timing precision, the value $\kappa = 3$, argued elsewhere to link energized vacuum BH interiors to accelerated cosmological expansion, can be excluded or detected for this $2.35^{+0.20}_{-0.18}\,M_\odot$ companion at $3\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ confidence by 2031 and 2036, respectively.

new.title: Improving On-board Shape Models Using Sun Sensors and Implicit Representations
new.summary: We propose an original, end-to-end approach to generate and refine the onboard 3D shape model of irregular small bodies, such as asteroids, using only low-cost Sun sensor eclipse data and coarse a priori knowledge, tailored for resource-constrained missions like CubeSats. Leveraging EclipseNets, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, our pipeline first refines 2D silhouettes by learning from real-time entry and exit events during spacecraft orbits, avoiding the limitations of traditional imaging or lidar in bandwidth-starved environments. These silhouettes then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations, enabling incremental updates to a high-fidelity implicit geometry representation capable of capturing fine-scale features and concavities. In simulations of the body Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, the method increases silhouette IoU from 0.70 to 0.87 and produces coherent 3D reconstructions, suggesting our approach could find a place in future autonomous architectures for small-body exploration.

new.title: Testing the Universality of RAR Model with Constraints on Fermionic Dark Matter for M31
new.summary: The Ruffini--Argüelles--Rueda (RAR) model describes dark matter as a self-gravitating system of massive fermions in thermodynamic equilibrium within general relativity. It suggests a dual morphology in galaxies: a highly degenerate quantum core mimicking a central supermassive black hole, and a classical halo that explains galactic rotation curves. Earlier applications of the model to the Milky Way restricted the fermion mass to $mc^{2}=48\text{--}345~\text{keV}$, and the orbits of the S-stars around Sagittarius~A$^{\ast}$ (Sgr~A$^{\ast}$) favored $mc^{2}=56~\text{keV}$, whereas a recent thermodynamic stability analysis allows only $mc^{2}\approx194\text{--}387~\text{keV}$. In this work, we apply the RAR model to the Andromeda galaxy (M31), which hosts a dark compact object of approximately $1.4\times10^{8}~M_{\odot}$ within $0.19~\text{pc}$, roughly 33 times the mass of Sgr~A$^{\ast}$. We solve the relativistic equilibrium equations for $mc^{2}=6\text{--}60~\text{keV}$. For all these masses, the fermionic core lies within $0.19~\text{pc}$ and provides the central mass without a black hole. With a bulge and disk added, the total rotation curve is statistically acceptable ($\chi^{2}/N_{\text{dof}}\approx1.18$) but lies below the disk data at $3\text{--}11~\text{kpc}$, an offset attributed to the baryonic models we adopted. The Navarro--Frenk--White (NFW) and Burkert profiles fitted to the same data give a lower $\chi^{2}$ but require an additional black hole. The stability of the M31 core against gravitational collapse limits the fermion mass to $mc^{2}\lesssim60~\text{keV}$. With the earlier Milky Way range, a single fermion can therefore describe both galaxies only for $mc^{2}=48\text{--}60~\text{keV}$, which includes $56~\text{keV}$. With the thermodynamic range, no fermionic core can supply the central mass of M31, so M31 would have to host a black hole.

new.title: Eos: a merger-induced starburst at the dawn of Galactic low-$α$ disc formation
new.summary: The last significant merger of the Milky Way, the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GS/E), is thought to have reshaped the early Galaxy and to mark the transition from the high-$\alpha$ to the low-$\alpha$ disc. The stars formed in situ during this merger offer a direct record of that epoch but are hard to identify. Using APOGEE DR17 abundances, we study Eos, a population of in-situ low-$\alpha$ stars on halo-like, non-rotating, eccentric orbits. The metal-poor part of Eos has a nitrogen dispersion as large as that of the pre-disc Aurora population and up to 1.7 times that of the low-$\alpha$ disc at the same metallicity. Heating alone cannot produce this: the Splash, a disc heated onto halo orbits by the same merger and selected in the same way, shows no excess over its parent disc. This part of Eos was therefore born in poorly mixed gas. Eos is also chemically intermediate between the accreted GS/E debris and the coeval in-situ Milky Way stars, and stars with more GS/E-like chemistry move on more extended orbits. Its stars are older than the bulk of the low-$\alpha$ disc but younger than the high-$\alpha$ disc and the Splash. We compare these observations with a merger-induced starburst seen in an Auriga simulation. There, a GS/E-like merger funnels the stripped progenitor gas into a mixing lane of intermediate metallicity, where stars form with intermediate abundances, a large chemical dispersion and a chemodynamical gradient set by their birth site, reproducing the observed signatures of Eos. We therefore interpret Eos as the surviving relic of the GS/E merger-induced starburst, born largely from the partially mixed gas bridging the two galaxies and marking the onset of the Milky Way's low-$\alpha$ disc. Eos thus provides a direct observational view of the star formation and galaxy evolution driven by the Milky Way's last significant merger.

new.title: The OGLE Collection of Variable Stars. Over 1.3 Million Human-Verified Eclipsing and Ellipsoidal Binaries in the Milky Way
new.summary: We present a new release of the OGLE collection of eclipsing and ellipsoidal binary systems in the Galactic bulge and disk. The catalog contains 1 330 024 objects, including 1 280 765 eclipsing binaries and 49 259 ellipsoidal variables, nearly three times as many systems as the previous editions of the OGLE collection. The selection and classification process involved expert visual inspection of the light curves. The catalog incorporates all available OGLE-II, OGLE-III, and OGLE-IV photometry, extending the observational baseline to nearly 28 years for some objects. The orbital periods and other observational parameters of previously known systems have been updated. We present basic statistics of the sample and highlight selected rare and unusual systems.

new.title: Top-heavy Initial Mass Functions are not enough at cosmic dawn
new.summary: A top-heavy stellar initial mass function (IMF) has been proposed to explain the unexpected abundance of ultraviolet (UV)-bright galaxies at cosmic dawn. We test this possibility using the metallicity-dependent, top-heavy IMF recently proposed by Chon et al. (2024), which is motivated by simulations of metal-poor star formation. We compare this IMF with a Salpeter IMF, self-consistently including the associated changes in UV emission, supernova feedback, metal enrichment, and dust production. At fixed star formation rate, the Chon IMF enhances the intrinsic UV luminosity by a factor ${B}_{1500}\simeq4.7$-$2.8$ over halo masses $M_h=10^{8-12}\,M_\odot$. However, its larger supernova rate suppresses star formation and increases dust attenuation, reducing the net boost to ${B}_{\rm UV}\simeq2.0$-$1.06$. For halos relevant to the bright end of the UV luminosity function, the enhancement is only ${B}_{\rm UV}\simeq1.2$-$1.4$, or about $0.3$ mag. Calculations with the DELPHI semi-analytic model confirm that the self-consistent Chon and Salpeter UV luminosity functions differ by less than $0.5$ dex at $z\simeq11$-$17$. Thus, a top-heavy IMF alone cannot explain the bright galaxy excess. Conversely, the predicted pair-instability supernova abundance differs by factors of $2$-$6$ between the two IMFs, providing a potentially cleaner observational diagnostic of the high-mass stellar populations at these early epochs.

new.title: Influence of variable IMF on the dynamical black hole mass estimates in massive ETGs
new.summary: Several studies have shown that the stellar initial mass function (IMF) in massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) is not universal. Recent results from stellar population synthesis models, based on integral-field unit (IFU) observations, indicate that the IMF varies radially, becoming increasingly bottom-heavy towards galaxy centres. This radial variation alters the stellar mass-to-light ratio ($\rm M_{*}/L$) and can significantly affect dynamical black hole (BH) mass estimates in massive ETGs. In this study, we investigate the impact of a radially varying IMF on BH mass estimates for five massive galaxies: NGC3923, NGC4261, NGC4636, IC4296, and IC4329. Using DYNAMITE, a triaxial Schwarzschild orbit-based modelling code, we perform mass modelling of these galaxies based on MUSE and SINFONI IFU observations. Our models incorporate radially varying stellar $\rm M_{*}/L$ profiles derived from spatially resolved stellar population modelling with a free IMF, and we compare the resulting BH masses with those obtained from dynamical models assuming a constant stellar $\rm M_{*}/L$. All galaxies in our sample show bottom-heavy IMFs in their central regions, with the IMF generally becoming lighter towards larger radii. We obtain constrained BH masses for NGC3923 and IC4329, while only upper limits are obtained for NGC4261, NGC4636, and IC4296. Compared with the constant-$\rm M_{*}/L$ models, the variable-$\rm M_{*}/L$ models yield BH masses lower by approximately 83% and 11% for NGC3923 and IC4329, respectively, while the BH mass upper limits for the other galaxies can increase or decrease. Our results demonstrate that spatial variations in the IMF and stellar $\rm M_{*}/L$ can have a non-negligible but strongly galaxy-dependent impact on dynamical BH mass measurements. These results highlight the importance of accounting for such variations in future dynamical modelling efforts.

new.title: Simulation-based inference for gravitational-wave cosmology: parameter reconstruction of a first-order electroweak phase transition
new.summary: The detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) from a cosmological first- order phase transition would be unambiguous evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model, with a strong electroweak phase transition (EWPT) at LISA as a prime example. Reconstructing the underlying model from such a signal is challenging, since the map from the model parameters to the spectrum is degenerate and strong transitions occupy only small and sparse regions of parameter space. We show that simulation-based inference (SBI), a likelihood-free approach applicable to generic SGWB sources, provides a reliable parameter reconstruction despite these difficulties. We first apply SBI to the thermodynamic parameters characterizing the transition, namely its strength, inverse duration, temperature and bubble wall velocity. As a concrete application, we then consider a strong EWPT in a singlet extension of the Standard Model and reconstruct the model parameters from the resulting SGWB. We find that the SBI posteriors agree with those of a likelihood-based Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis, at negligible cost per data set once the network has been trained. Using the network posterior as the proposal for importance sampling with the exact likelihood further corrects its remaining deviations, at a sampling efficiency several orders of magnitude higher than sampling from the prior. SBI thus offers a fast and flexible framework for the cosmological science case of LISA

new.title: Twisted resonant orbits: Quantifying the deceleration of the Galactic bar
new.summary: Recent structural discoveries in Gaia Data Release 3 reveal distinct, chevron-shaped over-densities in the radial phase space of the halo. Although initial interpretations identify these features as the phase-mixed relics of a past galaxy merger, their prominent asymmetry and persistence at high metallicities strongly challenge this interpretation. These features are better explained as a dynamical response to a Galactic bar, where stars are trapped in resonances. We establish the fractional $v_r$ asymmetry of the chevrons as a quantitative diagnostic tool for the bar's rotational state. We utilise test-particle simulations of a Milky Way-like galaxy to model various bar pattern speed evolutions, including decelerating and constant speed scenarios. By mapping the fractional asymmetry of the phase-space chevrons across a parameter space of bar deceleration rates and pattern speeds, we establish a direct correlation between the bar's deceleration and the rotational response of the resonant orbits. Comparing these simulated constraints with observational data from Gaia DR3 provides a framework for measuring the current deceleration of the Galactic bar, and a probe of the amount of dynamical friction occurring between the baryonic and dark matter content of the Milky Way. We find a dimensionless deceleration parameter $\eta \equiv - \dot{\Omega}_b/\Omega_b^2 = 0.0015^{+0.0016}_{-0.0009}$, equivalent to $\dot{\Omega}_b = -2.23^{+1.50}_{-2.46} \, \text{km s}^{-1} \text{kpc}^{-1} \text{Gyr}^{-1}$, in agreement with previous estimates obtained with independent methods. Gaia DR4 should sharpen this measurement considerably.

new.title: Ram Pressure Is Unable to Strip All Phases of the Interstellar Medium out of Spirals Falling into Galaxy Clusters
new.summary: Following the expansion of the Universe, spiral galaxies may fall at large speeds into galaxy clusters. Their interaction with the intracluster medium (ICM) may remove part of their gas and reduce their capacity for making new stars, as envisaged by Gunn & Gott. Ram pressure stripping (RPS) is commonly invoked to explain this gas loss and the wakes or tails left behind in-falling galaxies. Here we revise the impact of RPS on individual dense clouds and particularly focus on turbulent viscous stripping (TVS), driven by Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities at the cloud-ICM interface, that affects the high-density and low-temperature molecular gas. For an extended gaseous body to decelerate, momentum from its exposed surface must be communicated into the gas by a hydrodynamic disturbance able to propagate through it. Three-dimensional hydrodynamic calculations follow this interaction with dense clouds. At cloud number densities $n_{\mathrm{cl}}=10^2$ cm$^{-3}$, ram pressure acting through the transmitted shock strongly compresses and deforms the cloud and produces only a small deceleration; at $n_{\mathrm{cl}}=10^3$ cm$^{-3}$, the slower transmitted shock produces much weaker deformation. At both cloud densities, TVS continuously removes gas from the cloud surface and forms qualitatively indistinguishable trailing wakes, with comparable mass-loss rates, suggesting that TVS acting on individual dense clouds can generate filamentary substructure within jellyfish-galaxy tails.

new.title: Validation and Physical Characterization of Seven TESS Exoplanets: A Compact Multi-Planet System and Targets for Atmospheric Spectroscopy
new.summary: The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) continues to identify thousands of transit candidates that require statistical validation to rule out astrophysical false positives before atmospheric characterization can be pursued. We statistically validate and characterize seven TESS exoplanet candidates orbiting five host stars. As a consistency check of our automated vetting and Bayesian inference pipeline, we include TOI-2392.03, a sub-Neptune companion previously validated in the literature. Our framework combines automated signal retrieval, pixel-level centroid and Gaia DR3 contamination analysis, and false positive probability (FPP) computation with the TRICERATOPS vetting engine. Physical and orbital parameters are derived via nested sampling (juliet/Dynesty), complemented by an empirical mass-radius relation, since no dynamical mass measurements are available. Applying the same procedure to all candidates, we statistically validate six new exoplanets ($\mathrm{FPP} < 0.015$ and $\mathrm{NFPP} < 0.001$), one of which (TOI-7721.01) lies close to the FPP threshold. We report the period ratios of the three-planet system TOI-2392, and identify TOI-7721.01 and TOI-1277.02 as the candidates with the highest Transmission Spectroscopy Metrics (TSM) in our sample, making them targets of interest for atmospheric follow-up with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the upcoming Ariel mission.

new.title: EuclidFM: Foundation Model for Compact Photometric Survey Representation
new.summary: We present EuclidFM, a compact self-supervised model that learns object-level representations from heterogeneous catalogue photometry in Euclid Quick Data Release 1. Using 90,258 sources across three Euclid Deep Fields, a masked-autoencoder Transformer reconstructs withheld fluxes and uncertainties from available measurements, producing a 128-dimensional embedding per source. The embeddings encode morphological and photometric information: sources with high point-like probability have, on average, 12.4 similarly classified neighbours among their 15 nearest neighbours, compared with 4.3 under field- and magnitude-stratified randomization. Linear models trained on frozen embeddings predict VIS magnitudes with correlations of 0.954-0.980 across three held-out fields. For sources with VIS aperture-flux uncertainties up to 1 microJy, incorporating embeddings reduces the root-mean-square error in predicted log uncertainty by at least 24% relative to a magnitude-only model. A classifier trained on spectroscopically confirmed sources identifies 1,150 quasar candidates, but only 21 of the 156 candidates with accepted external counterparts show AGN evidence, including 12 spectroscopic quasars. The classifier's transferability to the wider photometric catalogue therefore remains uncertain, and its purity and completeness require further evaluation. Independently of classification, EuclidFM provides a common representation for downstream survey analyses when photometric coverage differs between sources. Code and data are available at this https URL .

new.title: Kinetic Tomography with Diffuse Interstellar Bands in APOGEE DR17
new.summary: Context: Mapping gas flows in the interstellar medium is key to understanding the formation of structure in our Milky Way. Methods that simultaneously reconstruct clouds' distances and line-of-sight velocities are called kinetic tomography (KT). Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) are powerful tracers for such maps because they trace the integrated dust density and the dust-weighted velocity. Previous DIB-KT works had small samples with coarse kpc-scale resolution and could not capture vertical disk structure. Aims: Make 4D (3D position + radial velocity) maps of the Milky Way from new, high-quality 15,273 Å DIB detections in APOGEE DR17. Methods: We combine variational inference and Gaussian processes with a mixture likelihood for low signal-to-noise detections and marginalization over distance uncertainties. We calibrate the model on mock fields and spectral injection tests and validate the map against independent tracers of the dust density (3D dust maps) and velocity substructure (masers and young stellar clusters). Results: We recover a posterior distribution over 3D maps of the density and velocity structure of the 15,273 Å DIB within 6 kpc of the Sun. We measure the large-scale structure of the DIB disk (scale length, height and flare) and detect vertical distortions consistent with the warp. On smaller scales, the map resolves distance ambiguities in gas longitude-velocity diagrams. From the second-order velocity structure function, we measure a slope (0.64 $\pm$ 0.04) consistent with Kolmogorov turbulence, amplitude consistent with expectations for molecular clouds, and a preliminary ratio of compressive-to-solenoidal modes. Conclusions: With larger DIB catalogs expected from SDSS-V, this framework should resolve kinematic substructure at the scales needed to constrain the formation and dynamics of individual clouds and voids. new.title: Off-Nuclear AGN Signatures in MaNGA: Spatially resolved selection using MEGACUBES
new.summary: We present a spatially resolved search for off-nuclear active galactic nucleus (AGN) candidates in the MaNGA survey. Using megacubes, we analyze over 10,000 galaxies, separating AGN activity from diffuse ionized gas with refined equivalent-width and surface-brightness thresholds. Combining a spatial radial algorithm with BPT, WHaN, and WHaD diagnostics, we classify 261 nuclear AGNs, 201 off-nuclear AGNs, and 159 'quiet' (composite-spaxel-dominated) sources. We test whether off-nuclear AGNs reside in distinct host galaxies or whether the offset is a local, gas-driven phenomenon. Nuclear and off-nuclear AGN hosts are statistically indistinguishable in stellar mass, age, star formation rate, and gas-phase metallicity. However, the excitation and kinematics of the AGN-ionized gas differ significantly: nuclear AGN spaxels have [O III]$\lambda5007$ luminosities $\sim 0.7$ dex higher than off-nuclear spaxels, whose lower [O III]/H$\beta$ ratios indicate genuinely lower-excitation gas rather than an obscured view of the central engine. We also find an orientation trend: 72% of nuclear hosts are face-on, versus 50% of off-nuclear hosts, so projection effects contribute to, but do not fully explain, off-nuclear detections. The classical WHaN boundary at $\log$([N II]/H$\alpha$) = -0.4 misclassifies high-metallicity diffuse ionized gas in integral field data; an empirical shift to -0.25 removes over 48,000 spurious AGN spaxels. Finally, the off-nuclear fraction implies an episodic AGN phase lifetime of $\sim 5 \times 10^4$ yr, consistent within a factor of a few with independent fading-AGN estimates and supporting short, recurrent accretion bursts.

new.title: Spiral Pitch Angles in Black Hole Images and Movies
new.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has produced images of M87* and Sgr A*, and will soon produce time sequences of images, or movies. General relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) models predict EHT sources will exhibit brightness fluctuations along the ring. The fluctuations are commonly connected to trailing spiral features. Here, we introduce a method to measure the pitch angle $\psi$ of radially extended features by cross-correlating brightness fluctuations sampled on rings at two distinct impact parameters. Pitch angle can be reliably measured from synthetic movies with BHEX resolution, and can be constrained even at EHT resolution. Single images enable noisy constraints of $\psi$. Pitch angle depends most on the viewing inclination and black hole spin. For constant inclination, the spiral winding direction depends on the sign of spin, with spirals winding more tightly in the direction of frame dragging near the horizon. The pitch angle will complement other observables to reliably constrain both the source inclination and spin in future analysis by EHT, and by expansions to the EHT such as ngEHT and BHEX.

new.title: Revealing galaxy assembly bias with luminosity-weighted marked correlations
new.summary: We investigate whether luminosity-weighted marked correlation functions can reveal secondary halo information beyond that encoded by halo mass alone, as expected in scenarios of galaxy assembly bias. We propose a controlled null test in which galaxy luminosities follow the same mean luminosity--halo mass relation and scatter, while their residuals are either (A) uncorrelated with secondary halo properties or (B) correlated with a standardized secondary halo property, $s$. Both models have identical halo occupation, galaxy positions, luminosity function, and unweighted projected two-point correlation function, $w_p(r_p)$, so their distinction is encoded entirely in the luminosity marks. At leading order, the projected marked correlation function difference, $\Delta\mathcal{M}_p(r_p)$, scales as $\rho^2\sigma_{\log L}^2\xi_{ss}(r_p)$, where $\rho$ controls the coupling between the luminosity and secondary-property residuals, $\sigma_{\log L}$ is the scatter in log luminosity at fixed halo mass, and $\xi_{ss}$ describes the spatial correlation of the secondary property. We test this framework using a DESI-BGS mock catalogue over $0.1<z<0.4$. For the injected dependence, we detect a marked-clustering deviation over $0.11<r_p/(h^{-1}\,{\rm Mpc})<1.04$, obtaining $\chi^2=30.14$ relative to the null covariance. A one-parameter test rejects the mass-only hypothesis at greater than $5\sigma$ significance ($p=2.13\times10^{-7}$) for $|\rho|>0.63$. At fixed $\sigma_{\log L}=0.23$, correlations as weak as $|\rho|\simeq0.52$ remain detectable, with the results stable under variations in the HOD prescription and modelled galaxy selection effects. These results establish luminosity-weighted marked clustering as a sensitive null test for property-based galaxy assembly bias and secondary halo information hidden from unweighted two-point clustering.

Right: In Model B, the same luminosities are reassigned so that their residuals correlate with a secondary halo property. For visual clarity, this correlation is represented by placing the most luminous galaxies preferentially closer to the halo centre; the radial ordering is illustrative and can represent any property, such as concentration, formation history, or environment. The halo occupation and galaxy positions are identical in the two models, so their unweighted projected two-point correlation functions are the same. Their luminosity-weighted marked correlation functions can nevertheless differ because the luminosity marks contain different spatially correlated information.

new.title: A novel pathway to stellar-mass black hole growth: Re-accretion of gas from stellar wind bubbles
new.summary: The formation of high-mass stellar black holes (BHs) observed in mergers by gravitational wave observatories remains difficult to explain using standard models of stellar evolution. We investigate whether newly formed stellar-mass BHs in dense molecular clouds can significantly increase their final mass by accreting gas from pre-existing, wind-blown interstellar bubbles produced by their progenitor stars. We performed 1D and 3D hydrodynamic simulations of interstellar bubbles driven by stellar feedback, incorporating thermal conduction, radiative cooling, gravity, ionizing radiation, stellar winds, and supernova (SN) explosions. We modeled the subsequent accretion onto the central BH for two formation scenarios: core-collapse SN and direct collapse. Our parameter space study encompasses over 500 1D simulations, varying initial cloud densities, gravitational binding energies, progenitor masses ($40-257\,M_\odot$), and metallicities ($0.66\,Z_\odot$ and $0.016\,Z_\odot$), and tracks the bubble evolution for millions of years post-BH formation. Scenarios exhibiting significant re-accretion were further validated using high-resolution 3D simulations. Our simulations show that BHs formed via direct collapse from low-metallicity progenitors can accrete up to $6.9\,M_\odot$ of gas from massive inner shells formed by late-stage slow winds, resulting in final BH masses of up to $93\,M_\odot$. Conversely, we find no significant re-accretion in scenarios involving an SN explosion or high-metallicity progenitors; in these cases, fast winds or SN ejecta efficiently evacuate dense structures from the bubble interior, leaving behind a hot, low-density medium. [abridged] This mechanism may help explain the unexpectedly high masses of BHs observed in gravitational wave events.

new.title: On the High Eccentricity Orbit of 51 Eri b and Constraints on Interactions with a Second Companion
new.summary: The eccentricity of an exoplanet's orbit is a key observational quantity that can be used to infer its dynamical past and predict its future orbital evolution. Planets are expected to emerge from their protoplanetary cradles with roughly circular eccentricities, and non-circular eccentricites to arise from subsequent dynamical processing in the absence of the gas disk. We present an updated orbit for 51 Eridani b based on 5 years of 0.2 mas precision optical interferometry from VLTI/GRAVITY(+). This planet is young (${\sim}20\,\mathrm{Myr}$ old), temperate ($T_{\rm eff}\sim650\,\mathrm{K}$), and on a wide orbit ($a{=}9.36\,\mathrm{au}$) with an uncertain mass ($M_{\rm b}\leq12\,M_{\rm J}$). We measured the planet's motion to an exceptionally high precision, confirming that its orbit is very eccentric ($e_b=0.574\pm0.003$). We observe residuals to the absolute astrometry of the host star based on a single planet orbit that could be attributable to reflex motion from a third body in the system. We construct a two companion orbit model that could explain the apparent reflex motion of 51 Eri A: this model predicts that the putative second companion has $M_c\in[1.0, 2900]_{95\%}\,M_{\rm Jup}$ and $a_c\in[0.3, 3.1]_{95\%}\,\mathrm{au}$. In this framework, a dynamical interaction between b and ``c" could have kicked the exterior, lower mass b out onto its present, eccentric orbit. If this signal is astrophysical, and not due to a systematic error, this candidate should be confirmable with Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry in the near future.

new.title: Intra-day variability of the gamma-ray/optical emission of 3C 454.3: the complexity beyond the long-term correlation
new.summary: Simultaneous $\gamma$-ray/optical observations probe particle acceleration and radiative processes in blazar jets. The blazar 3C 454.3 shows a significant long-term correlation between these bands, often interpreted as support for the canonical one-zone leptonic emission model. However, both bands show strong intra-day variability, and whether the correlation persists during individual flares remains unclear. We study the $\gamma$-ray/optical correlation and intra-day variability of 3C 454.3 over 17 years (2007--2024), on timescales $\leq 24$ h. We analyse AGILE and Fermi-LAT observations using light curves binned from 3 to 48 h, together with simultaneous $R$-band photometry from WEBT and public optical data sets. We examine the flux and spectral evolution of individual flares, estimate time-dependent correlation properties, and derive Compton dominance from optical and $\gamma$-ray luminosities. We confirm the long-term correlation, but find large intrinsic dispersion and a slope of $\eta \simeq 1.6$--$1.7$, inconsistent with a single canonical one-zone scenario. On shorter timescales, correlation strengths range from weak to strong, with slopes spanning $\eta \simeq 0.4$--$2.0$. We also find orphan flares in both bands, diverse flare morphologies, distinct Compton-dominance patterns with rapid excursions from $\sim 10$ to 120, and heterogeneous spectral trends. The shortest resolved variability timescales ($t_{\rm var} \lesssim 3$ h) indicate that localized emission regions are required by causality. The $\gamma$-ray/optical correlation in 3C 454.3 thus arises not from a single emission regime, but from multiple epoch-dependent physical states. Increasing temporal resolution reveals richer variability, highlighting the importance of systematic intra-day, multi-epoch studies of bright FSRQs.

new.title: Where Did the Angular Momentum Go? WASP-12 b May Have Circularized on a Retrograde Orbit
new.summary: WASP-12 b is the only exoplanet with confirmed orbital decay. Angular momentum transferred from its decaying orbit should have realigned the star's thin convective layer, yet an earlier Rossiter--McLaughlin (RM) measurement suggested a $\sim$60$^\circ$ spin--orbit misalignment. We present two new Keck Planet Finder RM measurements. We measure a sky-projected obliquity of $\lambda=-1.3\pm8.7^\circ$; and the star's projected rotation velocity is $v\sin i_\star=1.3\pm0.1~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, an order of magnitude lower than expected for a star of its mass and age. With WASP-12's low chromospheric activity, $\log R^\prime_{\rm HK}=-5.5$, our analysis favors an aligned system in which $v\sin i_\star$ reflects slow surface rotation with $P_{\rm rot}\sim60$ days, rather than a projection effect. Our evolution models favor a late-main-sequence star rather than a subgiant, with a central convective core found in 99\% of posterior samples. This internal structure suppresses the central-focusing and nonlinear wave-breaking mechanisms for inward-propagating gravity waves. We propose that WASP-12 b was initially placed on a retrograde orbit after high-eccentricity migration, when its host rotated at $v\sin i_\star\approx14$~km~s$^{-1}$ (or $P_{\rm rot}\sim$6 days). Tidal decay transferred orbital angular momentum to the convective envelope, aligning the surface. The retrograde interior acts as an angular-momentum reservoir, while interior--envelope coupling slows the surface rotation. A semi-empirical relation gives an envelope--interior angular-momentum exchange timescale of $\sim4$~Myr, similar to the observed orbital-decay timescale of $\sim3.25$~Myr. The angular-momentum budget also permits this initially retrograde evolution. In contrast, an initially prograde planet would have spun up the surface rotation to a rate substantially higher than observed.

new.title: Rediscussion of eclipsing binaries. Paper 33. The A-type system CW Canis Majoris in the PLATO southern field
new.summary: CW CMa is a detached eclipsing binary containing two A0 V stars in a circular orbit of period 2.12 d. We analyse the light-curves of this system from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) together with published radial velocity measurements to determine the masses and radii of the component stars to high precision, obtaining masses of 2.087 +/- 0.022 Msun and 1.972 +/- 0.024 Msun, and radii of 1.841 +/- 0.012 Rsun and 1.748 +/- 0.014 Rsun. We detect a changing orbital period over the four available TESS sectors indicative of the presence of a companion on a wider orbit. We develop a new method to determine the effective temperatures of the component stars using their measured radii, the Gaia parallax, and surface-brightness calibrations to reduce the degeneracy between temperature and extinction. The method gives temperatures of 9850 +/- 280 K and 9570 +/- 270 K and an interstellar extinction of A(V) = 0.32 +/- 0.06 mag. The properties of the system can be matched by theoretical models for a subsolar metal abundance (Z = 0.010) and an age of 400 +/- 20 Myr. CW CMa has been selected as a target for the PLATO satellite, with which it will be observed for at least two years.

new.title: Multiphase Gas in High-$z$ Cosmic Sheets
new.summary: We present high-resolution cosmological simulations of individual cosmic sheets ($z=3-6$) using the moving-mesh code AREPO to study cold gas ($T\approx10^4\rm ~K$) in the diffuse cosmic web. We find cosmic sheet gas forms a fragmented morphology, evident as kiloparsec-scale variations in the neutral hydrogen column density ($N_{\rm HI}$). Fragmentation arises from the bending and disruption of the cold-dense sheet core into a multiphase medium. Nonlinear thin shell instability (NTSI) and later shear-induced vorticity drive this bending, rather than previously suggested thermal or Richtmyer-Meshkov instabilities. Higher resolution enhances fragmentation. Across a fourfold range in spatial resolution, $N_{\rm HI}$ covering fractions increase by factors of $\approx 1.5-3.5$ for partial Lyman-limit systems (pLLS) and Lyman-limit systems (LLS). An order-of-magnitude estimate suggests sheets may host a large fraction of the ultra-low metallicity (p)LLS population. Equivalent MP-Gadget simulations show qualitatively similar fragmentation, but numerical smoothing effects are present. Cosmic-sheet gas properties remain unconverged despite our high resolutions.

new.title: The HI Mass Fractions of Milky Way Analog Samples
new.summary: We estimate average HI mass fractions, f_HI = M_HI/M_star, for nine Milky Way analog samples (MWAs): galaxies selected on similarity to the MW in terms of various properties. We find most (seven) MWAs have lower <f_HI> than a recent estimate for the MW, although only the two largest have significantly lower estimates. We suggest that either the MW has an unusual f_HI for its properties, or we are overestimating its HI content, one of many challenging global measurements to make from our perspective inside our own Galaxy.

new.title: The SPACE Program IV: Atmospheric Features on the Cold Transiting Sub-Neptune TOI-6478 b
new.summary: Among the current population of exoplanets there are very few sub-Neptunes that have their atmospheric composition identified. This is primarily due to sub-Neptunes having high metallicity, clouds, and/or hazes obscuring absorption features. This often produces a spectrum that presents itself as a featureless spectrum especially in the near-IR. However, there are tentative trends that suggest sub-Neptunes with the lowest equilibrium temperatures ($\mathrm{T_{eq} < 400\:K}$) have detectable features, perhaps due to inefficient haze production or cloud sedimentation. TOI-6478 b is a low-density sub-Neptune exoplanet ($\rm <\mathrm{9.9\:M_{\oplus}}$ and $\rm \sim 4.5R_{\oplus}$) with an equilibrium temperature $\mathrm{T_{eq} = 220 \:K}$ assuming zero albedo. In this study, we present the highest S/N spectral feature ($\sim$6) of any sub-Neptune detected using HST/WFC3. We detect this spectral feature using a robust analysis that incorporates the Transit Light Source Effect (TLSE) to rule out false detections due to stellar activity. With the narrow bandpass of HST we were unable to distinguish whether the spectral feature at 1.4$\mu$m is from H$_2$O or CH$_4$ absorption. Meanwhile, self-consistent atmospheric models provide physical motivation for CH$_4$ to be the dominant absorber given that H$_2$O should condense or cold trap at higher pressures. Through our analysis we determine that HST/WFC3 alone cannot distinguish between major absorbers. However, a broader wavelength coverage by JWST will be able to measure the atmospheric composition in detail, due to the high S/N features for this target.

new.title: Transition Zone from ExoEarth to ExoVenus: Critical Insight from Planets on the Edge
new.summary: Venus and Earth, planets with similar masses and radii, provide astonishingly different environments, raising the question of why these two rocky worlds evolved so differently. Explaining this divergence is a central challenge in comparative planetology and astrobiology. Now, atmospheric studies of exoplanets can explore the possibilities of terrestrial planet evolution, especially in the era of JWST; however, we have not yet realized the critical insights rocky exoplanets in the Transition Zone (TZ) can provide. These TZ planets in the overlap between the Habitable Zone and Venus Zone can test how incident stellar irradiation affects surface water retention and habitability. Observations of exoplanets in the TZ can probe not only the emergence and decline of exoplanet habitability but also test hypotheses about Venus' past, complementing upcoming Venus flagship missions. Here, we analyze NASA's Exoplanet Archive, updated with Gaia DR3 data, and provide a target list of 23 rocky exoplanets in the Earth-to-Venus Transition Zone, along with 2 planets in the Venus Evolution Zone (EV). We examine their demographics and quantify their potential for follow-up observations. This list of rocky TZ and EV planets allows observers to optimize target selection and observing strategy for specific instruments. Characterizing exoplanets in the Transition Zone will be critical to investigating open questions about the emergence and decline of habitability on rocky worlds, the evolution from an exo-Earth to an exo-Venus, and Earth's future.

new.title: Sherlock 'Chrones: The Curious Case of NGC 6791 and Asteroseismic Targets Therein Reveals Mixing Length Dependence on Evolutionary Stage
new.summary: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory. The old, metal-rich, open cluster NGC 6791 is well studied, but the availability of asteroseismic observations of individual cluster members allows for a more in-depth analysis. Driven by mounting evidence that the solar assumption for convection used in almost all 1D stellar models is not adequate, and in light of the increased precision provided by modern data and asteroseismic constraints, we built and compared custom isochrones with varying values of the convective mixing length, $\alpha_\text{MLT}$, to two clusters with well-determined ages: NGC 6791 and the well-studied, metal-poor globular cluster M92. For both clusters, we found that the best-fitting mixing length parameter decreases monotonically as a function of evolutionary phase, finding values between $0.98-1.10\alpha_{\odot}$ for NGC 6791 and $1.16-1.21\alpha_{\odot}$ for M92. In NGC 6791, this corresponds to an 18% decrease in the best fitting mixing length between the main sequence turn-off and upper end of the red giant branch. The degree of variation found within this one object is therefore comparable to variation across the literature in $\alpha_\text{MLT}$ fits for other non-solar targets, calling single-valued $\alpha_\text{MLT}$ fits to clusters into question. It is also consistent with $\log g$-$\alpha_\text{MLT}$ trends predicted by higher-fidelity, 3D convection analyses. Our results therefore illustrate the need for more flexibility in our treatment of the mixing length in isochrones to properly model clusters.

new.title: 3D Binary Evolution of a Merging Binary Black Hole Progenitor
new.summary: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars. It is key to the production of gravitational waves through formation of binary black holes and other double compact objects. We integrate global 3D hydrodynamics into stellar evolutionary modeling to resolve mass transfer across nuclear timescales. We employ the shellular approximation in the stellar evolution code MESA to map a 3D spatial structure by equipotential shells in the Roche geometry to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally-distorted surfaces. We employ the method of time-incremented multiscale evolution to alternate between stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span large timescales with dynamical feedback. We employ this framework to examine a likely merging binary black hole progenitor system of a low-metallicity 30Msol donor star and 9.3Msol black hole from the end of the main sequence to core Carbon depletion. We modeled two complete mass transfer phases in 3D while self-consistently accounting for stellar evolution. These comprised a thermal-timescale early Case B phase and a nuclear-timescale late Case B phase. The prescription of Kolb & Ritter (1990) closely predicted the results of 3D evolution, except at the end of the first phase of mass transfer; our 3D model remained well-contained by the outer Lagrange point, despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow during this stage. We find incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly impact expected merger times. Our model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions. L2/L3 outflows formed even while underflowing those equipotentials. Our model suggests these outflows can be neglected for the evolution of similar systems, but were dense enough to potentially impact X-ray observations.

new.title: First $Ω_{\rm m}-w$ Measurement Using Only Fast Radio Burst Observations
new.summary: Though fast radio bursts (FRBs) are widely advocated as a dark energy probe, no valid $\Omega_m-w$ constraint has been obtained exclusively from FRB data to date. Benefiting from a rapidly growing localized sample and a novel statistical framework for modeling the dispersion measure (DM), we report the first simultaneous inference of the matter density $\Omega_m$ and dark energy equation of state parameter $w$ from FRBs alone, without external observational priors on these two parameters. We combine a multi-parameter emulator for the nonlinear matter power spectrum with a physically motivated electron prescription to construct a cosmology-dependent cosmic-DM distribution. Within this unified analysis framework, the mean and variance of DM respond self-consistently to the same underlying cosmology, directly connecting the FRB likelihood to both cosmic expansion and structure growth. Analyzing 125 localized FRBs at $0.105\leq z\leq2.148$, we obtain $\Omega_m = 0.33^{+0.10}_{-0.11}$ and $w = -0.80^{+0.28}_{-0.38}$ under the flat $w$CDM model. We find a new positive $\Omega_m-w$ degeneracy in the FRB posterior, opposite to the strong anticorrelation derived from Type Ia supernovae, offering a complementary test of dark energy properties and highlighting their potential in future precision cosmological studies.

new.title: Design and Forecasts for a Rubin Twilight Program for Nearby Type Ia Supernovae
new.summary: Nearby Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are important for supernova cosmology, but saturation in 30 s exposures, gaps in light-curve sampling, and the footprint of Vera C. Rubin Observatory's baseline Wide-Fast-Deep (WFD) survey limit the nearby sample. To improve the low-$z$ sample, we propose a twilight follow-up program using Rubin Observatory for 1-5 s griz exposures at solar altitudes $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -9^\circ$. Using simulations of one year of WFD observations, we find that twilight follow-up adds 230 quality-selected SNe Ia from an external sample drawn primarily from the Transient Name Server (TNS). At $z<0.08$, the usable sample increases from 368 to 643 SNe Ia, including 50 WFD events recovered by refitting their light curves with twilight photometry. Combining these twilight observations with high-redshift WFD and Deep Drilling Field samples increases the statistical-only dark-energy $(w_0,w_a)$ figure of merit from 49.3 to 58.3 (18%) and reduces $\sigma(w_a)$ by 10%. For measurements of structure growth at $0.02 \le z<0.06$, the fractional uncertainty on $f\sigma_8$ decreases from 0.783 to 0.305. Restricting the program to $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -11^\circ$ reduces the dark-energy improvement to 7.2%. These short exposures could also provide unsaturated photometry of potential distance-ladder calibrators at $z<0.02$.

new.title: FAST Burst-Cluster Catalog of FRB 20240114A
new.summary: We present the complete FAST burst-cluster catalog of FRB 20240114A, covering its 495-day active episode from January 28, 2024 to June 5, 2025. The catalog contains 13261 burst clusters, 19037 bursts, and 29026 sub-bursts detected in 99 observing sessions. The data reveal distinct organization across temporal scales. Among drifting burst clusters, downward-drifting clusters outnumber upward-drifting ones by approximately $9.4:1$. Between separate burst clusters, previously reported frequency changes show no preferred direction, while our Weibull analysis finds their arrival times broadly consistent with Poisson statistics, suggesting that burst clusters may represent approximately independent emission episodes within observing sessions. The Parkes/Murriyang observations revealed a long-term modulation of the characteristic emission frequency, and the extended FAST measurements show a consistent evolution. Burst energetics increase with cluster multiplicity and activity level, although significant scatter remains. The manually refined dispersion measure increases at $1.29\pm0.11\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}\,yr^{-1}}$, enlarging the still limited but growing sample of repeaters with increasing DM. Overall, these results summarize the spectral--temporal evolution of FRB 20240114A and present a burst-cluster catalog linked to the existing BurstID measurements, providing a basis for future studies of repeating FRBs.

new.title: The Cosmic Infrared Background from Population III.1 Supermassive Stars and Black Holes
new.summary: We investigate the cosmic infrared background (CIB) that is expected to arise from the Population (Pop) III.1 supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenario, which involves early SMBH seeding via supermassive primordial star formation enabled by dark matter annihilation heating. We model the emission from Pop III.1 supermassive stars, including their growth phase, flash ionization phase, and early black hole accretion phase, as well as accompanying emission from lower-mass Pop III.2 stars. The CIB is composed of stellar and SMBH accretion disk continuum radiation, nebular continuum emission, and Ly$\alpha$ radiation redistributed through scattering in the neutral intergalactic medium. Based on the feedback regulated Pop III.1 model of Petkova et al. (2026), our fiducial model assumes $\sim 10^5\,M_\odot$ Pop III.1 stars forming by $z_{\rm flash}=20$ with a comoving number density of $\sim0.2\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$. For this model, the combined stellar contribution is less than $1\%$ of existing direct and diffuse CIB measurements. However, the contribution to the CIB from $z\sim6-20$ SMBH accretion is expected to be larger than the Pop III.1 stellar component for average Eddington ratios $\lambda_{\text{Edd}} \sim 0.01$. Latest CIB observations place constraints of $\lambda_{\text{Edd}} \lesssim 0.3$ for the fiducial Pop III.1 model during these epochs.

new.title: Dark Matter Model Implications of a Candidate Sub-halo Near the Sun, and the Data Needed to Discriminate Among Them
new.summary: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo. We work out what such an object implies for the nature of dark matter, organizing the implications by their observable effect: suppression or enhancement of structure formation, internal structure and survival after formation, and emission or scattering by the constituents. We discuss ultralight wave dark matter, thermal and nonthermal warm dark matter, dark acoustic oscillations and dark matter-baryon scattering, elastic and inelastic self-interactions, invisible decays with recoil, primordial black holes, indirect detection, and a possible connection to the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy recoil candidate. We then ask what new data would discriminate among these models. The existing accelerations are measured outside the tidal radius, where they are blind to the interior mass distribution, to the object's velocity, and to the sub-halo population. We identify four routes that lift these degeneracies: accelerations measured inside the halo, which separate point-mass, cuspy, and cored profiles; lensing and accretion, which test whether the mass is compact; the morphology of annihilation or decay emission, which probes the inner profile; and a search for a comoving stellar population, which tests whether the object is dark and measures its velocity. We also contrast this program with pulsar-timing-array searches for transiting dark matter substructure, which probe vastly lighter objects through a different observable.

new.title: A Shallow Phase-resolved Gamma-Ray Luminosity-Cutoff Energy Relation in Globular Cluster Millisecond Pulsars
new.summary: Globular clusters (GCs) provide dense stellar environments for investigating the high-energy emission of millisecond pulsars (MSPs). Using $\sim$17.3~yr of \textit{Fermi}-LAT Pass~8 data in the 0.1-500.0~GeV range, we study four MSPs that dominate, or contribute substantially to, the GeV $\gamma$-ray emission of their host GCs. Significant off-pulse $\gamma$-ray emission is detected from PSR~J1823$-$3021A, J1824$-$2452A, and J1835$-$3259B. For these sources, the cutoff energy, $E_{\rm cut}$, varies systematically with rotational phase and is positively correlated with the phase-resolved energy flux. Using the phase-resolved isotropic $\gamma$-ray luminosity ($L_{\gamma}$), we find $L_{\gamma}\propto E_{\rm cut}^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha=0.74^{+0.16}_{-0.14}$. This slope is substantially shallower than that reported for field MSPs, $\alpha=2.31^{+0.22}_{-0.25}$, and the $\alpha=16/7\simeq2.29$ scaling expected for curvature radiation in the equatorial current sheet framework. The origin of the shallow relation remains uncertain, potentially reflecting cluster-associated $\gamma$-ray emission, differences in emission geometry and beaming, or limited photon statistics. Our results demonstrate that GC MSPs provide valuable targets for testing phase-resolved high-energy emission physics in dense stellar environments.

new.title: Model-Based Low-Order Wavefront Sensing and Control with a Fully Physical Digital Twin on MagAO-X
new.summary: Context. Residual low-order aberrations and post-AO tip-tilt jitter are major drivers of stellar leakage in small-inner-working-angle coronagraphs and limit high-contrast imaging performance. Aims. The aim of this work is to develop a fully physical and differentiable digital twin for the focal plane low-order wavefront sensor on MagAO-X. This digital twin can be used to provide accurate non-linear and fast linearised wavefront sensing and control to deal with low-order aberrations. Methods. We build a physics-based optical model of the focal plane low order wavefront sensor (FLOWFS) system and calibrate it using laboratory and on-sky measurements. The calibrated model is used for non-linear phase retrieval, deriving a model-based linear reconstructor, and generating the corresponding reference image for real-time control. Results. The calibrated digital twin accurately reproduces the sensor response and recovers the dominant low-order aberrations. In the laboratory, non-linear reconstruction achieves residual floors of about 6 to 7 nm over the pupil, compared with about 11 nm for the linear reconstructor, and the same digital-twin framework transfers across different coronagraph and wavelength configurations. On-sky, the model can be recalibrated with limited changes, achieves reconstruction performance close to the residual atmospheric floor, and provides a linear reconstructor that enables stable closed-loop low-order control at kHz speed. Conclusions. A fully physical digital twin can unify accurate low-order wavefront reconstruction, fast linearised control, and transfer across observing configurations and from lab to on-sky operation within a single interpretable framework.

new.title: The Universality of Halo Growth and Merger Rates in Modified Gravity Theories
new.summary: In the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework, the merger rate of dark matter haloes has been found to follow a nearly universal form, with only weak dependence on halo mass and redshift. We examine whether this universality is preserved in modified gravity (MG) models, where the growth of cosmic structure can deviate from that of general relativity (GR). We use the ELEPHANT suite of large $N$-body simulations to study halo merger rates and mass accretion histories in different modified gravity models, including two representative scenarios beyond-GR: the Hu--Sawicki chameleon $f(R)$ model and the normal branch of the Dvali--Gabadadze--Porrati model. For the mass accretion histories, the modified gravitational effect can produce systematic departures from GR, generally corresponding to more rapid halo growth. The deviations are relatively small when the MG effect is weak, while they become more pronounced in models with strong deviation from GR and can exceed $15\%$ in the extreme case. For the halo merger rate, we find that the nearly universal behavior is well preserved across all the gravity models, with only weak dependence on redshift and halo mass, reflecting the unbiased accretion nature of halo growth. However, apparent deviation from this universality can arise if the halo mass is not defined consistently with the modified gravity model.

new.title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks
new.summary: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.

new.title: TWIN-2: Timing Solar Radio Bursts between 180-350 MHz Against GOES and Aditya-L1 X-ray Detections
new.summary: We have conducted continuous solar observations for approximately two and half years using the Two-Element Interferometer (TWIN) at Gauribidanur Radio Observatory (RRI). During which several solar events have been detected. Our observational period coincides with the maximum events phase of the Solar Cycle 25, providing us opportunity to analyse the evolution of the solar activity. Our analysis of two and half years data show a clear increase in the occurrences of solar events, which is consistent with the expected rise in the solar activity towards the peak phase of the Solar Cycle 25. We further investigate the detected solar radio events using X-ray observations from the space based Aditya-L1 and the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) satellites. For the automated detection of SRBs, a machine learning suite has been trained. This also serves as an instrument for space weather monitoring. On the 7th of November 2025, a solar storm was detected by our pipeline in realtime. A brief overview of the data-processing pipeline, along with the RFI mitigation techniques employed to identify and characterize the solar events, is also presented. Observation data of two and a half years of TWIN is available for public access. The data has been used in student training programmes on solar radio data analysis, with students carrying out the analysis and contributing to the initial analysis of the detected events.

new.title: False Periodicities in Repeating Fast Radio Bursts Caused by Burst Clustering
new.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients with high brightness temperatures, but their physical origin remains uncertain. The association of FRB 200428 with a Galactic magnetar provides compelling evidence that at least some FRBs originate from magnetar-like systems. Nevertheless, periodic modulation associated with neutron-star rotation has not been robustly detected in extragalactic FRBs. Motivated by the reported 1.7 s periodicity in the active repeater FRB 20201124A, we conduct a systematic search for short-timescale periodicity in four highly active repeating FRB sources. We employ a sliding-window method that analyzes temporally adjacent bursts within restricted time intervals, allowing transient or intermittent periodic signals to be identified. The search yields apparent period candidates with nominal Poisson-calibrated significances comparable to that reported for the 1.7 s signal, although the inferred periods vary substantially among sources and observing windows. We then perform a nonparametric waiting-time randomization test, in which the observed waiting-time distribution is preserved while the temporal ordering is destroyed. The randomized sequences reproduce the main candidate-period structures seen in the data, demonstrating that these apparent periodicities can arise from the non-Poissonian waiting-time statistics rather than from a coherent periodic process. Rotation-modulated epidemic-type aftershock sequence simulations provide a complementary parametric illustration of the same effect. We therefore find no robust evidence for a short intrinsic periodicity in these data, and the reported 1.7 s signal is not uniquely distinguished from clustering-induced candidates. Robust periodicity searches must evaluate significance against null models that account for the observed waiting-time statistics and the full search procedure.

new.title: New Candidate Activity Periods from FRB 20240209A and Repeating Fast Radio Burst Sources in the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
new.summary: Repeating fast radio burst (FRB) sources with periodic activity provide important constraints on FRB models invoking neutron-star precession, rotation, or orbital modulation in binary systems. Although a few FRB sources exhibit evidence of periodic behavior, it remains unclear whether periodic activity is a common underlying feature of repeating FRBs. Using a new FRB periodicity search pipeline introduced by A. B. Pearlman et al. (2026), which is optimized for sparse event-arrival-time data from FRB surveys, we search for activity periods in the burst arrival times from FRB 20240209A and repeating FRBs in the Second Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME)/FRB Catalog. For FRB 20240209A, we identify a new candidate activity period of 170.4 $\pm$ 4.7 days, with a trials-corrected statistical significance of 5.3$\sigma$. Our larger burst sample shows no evidence of the 128.5-day activity period previously reported for this source by A. Pal (2025). We also report candidate activity periods of 28.46 $\pm$ 0.08 days, 86.7 $\pm$ 0.5 days, and 36.4 $\pm$ 0.5 days for FRB 20190208A, FRB 20200926A, and FRB 20220529A, with trials-corrected statistical significances of 3.1$\sigma$, 4.0$\sigma$, and 3.5$\sigma$, respectively. All statistical significances are evaluated against a homogeneous (constant-rate) Poisson null hypothesis, and we caution that they may decrease under null models that incorporate burst clustering. Collectively, our results constitute the most comprehensive search for periodic activity in the repeating FRB population to date.

new.title: The Atmospheric Circulation of Cloudy Hot and Ultra-hot Jupiters: the Need for Dissipation of Large-scale Flows to Reduce the Nightside Brightness Temperatures of Ultra-hot Jupiters
new.summary: We perform general circulation modeling of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across equilibrium temperatures of T_eq=1600 to 2800 K, incorporating cloud formation and its feedback on atmospheric dynamics. This study specifically examines whether clouds explain the systematically low nightside brightness observed in Spitzer thermal phase curves of ultra-hot Jupiters. We found that clouds generally increase phase-curve amplitudes and reduce eastward offsets, and these effects are most pronounced at relatively low T_eq and gradually weaken as T_eq increases. We discussed two mechanisms responsible for reducing the phase-curve offsets by clouds: the dynamical and geometric effects. Without explicit dissipation of large-scale winds, strong equatorial jets develop, maintaining a hot equatorial region and clearing clouds near the nightside equator at T_eq >= 2200 K, with thick clouds instead forming mainly at mid-to-high latitudes. These patchy nightside clouds do not sustain low nightside fluxes as temperatures rise, suggesting that clouds alone cannot explain the observed nightside brightness for ultra-hot Jupiters. Strong dissipation, parameterized as magnetic drags, suppresses equatorial jets and promotes nightside cloud coverage. In both clear and cloudy models, drag weakens the dependence of Spitzer nightside brightness temperature on equilibrium temperature; clouds further lower the nightside brightness temperature with the same drag prescription. Clouds also dampen amplitudes of thermal spectra on the nightside and, under small-particle conditions, can even produce emission features. Due to limited dayside cloud cover, our models yield negligible Bond albedos. Finally, interpreting simulated thermal phase curves with energy balance models in near-IR and IR bands tends to overestimate the Bond albedos of ultra-hot Jupiters by an order of magnitude or more.

new.title: The non-equilibrium state of the Galactic disk $-$ new insights from GALAH DR4
new.summary: The non-equilibrium state of the Galactic disk has drawn extensive attention since ESA's \textit{Gaia} launch. Complex structure appears across a multi-parameter space of stellar abundances, ages, and kinematics. Using GALAH DR4, we investigate ridge and phase-spiral structures in chemical-abundance, phase ($v_i,x_i$), action--angle ($J_i,\theta_i$), and frequency--action ($\Omega_i,J_i$) spaces ($i=R,\phi,z$). Our sample includes 333,412 disk stars with reliable chemodynamical data. In the $R$--$v_\phi$ plane, ridges trace near-constant $J_\phi$ tracks and show coherent variations in $\theta_R$ and $\theta_\phi$. In $J_\phi$--$J_R$, ridges are most prominent when encoded by $z_{\rm max}$ and preferentially associate with metal-rich, low-$\alpha$ populations. In the solar neighbourhood ($R=7.2$--$9.2$\,kpc), we recover a clear phase spiral in $z$--$v_z$. Encoded in $v_\phi$, $\Omega_R$, or $\Omega_\phi$, one-armed spirals appear, whereas the $v_R$-encoded map shows a two-armed spiral. Projecting actions onto $z$--$v_z$ reveals residual spiral signatures in $J_R$ and $J_\phi$, indicating that the phase spiral encodes in-plane orbital information. Both structures depend on age: ridges remain at similar locations with varying contrast, while the phase spiral is more tightly wound in younger and more loosely wound in older populations. Several ridges correspond in $J_\phi$ to known moving groups, and excluding stars in all six moving-group regions makes the phase spiral less distinct in mean radial velocity maps. These links support interpreting ridges, phase spirals, and moving groups within a common phase-space dynamical framework. Combined with trends in orbital properties, age, and abundance, these findings suggest a common dynamical origin and distinct chemodynamical responses of a perturbed Galactic disk.

new.title: Hard X-ray flux rope anchor points in the October 2024 X9 flare
new.summary: In recent studies, signatures of non-thermal hard X-ray (HXR) emission at the anchor point of erupting flux ropes were reported, suggesting that accelerated electrons trapped in the erupting flux ropes can reach the chromosphere and produce Bremsstrahlung emission there. We investigated the HXR sources observed during the impulsive phase of the X9-class flare SOL2024-10-03T12:18 from AR 13842 and assessed whether any of the HXR sources are associated with the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. We analysed the evolution and location of the flare ribbon sources and coronal dimmings to diagnose the eruption process by using multi-vantage point data from the Solar Orbiter and Earth-orbiting instruments. We combined this with a pre-eruption non-linear force-free magnetic field extrapolation to reconstruct the initial magnetic connectivity and compare it to the observed flare ribbons and dimming locations. The magnetic field extrapolation shows two flux ropes before the flare onset. Tether-cutting reconnection during the impulsive phase of the flare results in a larger erupting flux rope formed by the reconnection of the two pre-existing flux ropes. The Spectrometer/Telescope for Imaging X-rays on Solar Orbiter observes at least four distinct HXR sources: two flare footpoints and two additional outer sources at the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. These observations corroborate earlier speculations that non-thermal electrons trapped in the erupting flux rope precipitate along the field lines into the denser chromosphere.

new.title: Square Kilometre Array Science Data Challenge 3b: EoR inference
new.summary: We present and analyse the results of Science Data Challenge 3b (SDC3b; this https URL ), an Epoch of Reionization (EoR) inference exercise organised by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) using simulated SKA data. The nine-month challenge, running from October 2024 to May 2025, represents the first community-wide comparison of EoR inference pipelines on common simulated datasets. We consider multiple datasets designed to assess performance on both foreground-free and foreground-contaminated cylindrical power spectra and imaging products, adopting different reionization scenarios and EoR simulation models. We include results from 16 teams, which employ a range of methodologies to infer the posterior distribution of the hydrogen neutral fraction across three redshift intervals spanning z=8.41 to z=6.25. The results show significant inter-team variability of the astrophysical constraints even in the simpler case where only instrumental noise is added to the cosmological signal. This underscores the need for further investigation into the relative contributions of signal modelling, the treatment of instrumental effects, and inference methods to the robustness of the resulting conclusions. Although individual methods can produce biased parameter estimates, the combined average of their estimates remains close to the input values, suggesting that independent approaches can offset method-specific biases.

new.title: The origin of the apparent ULX deficit in NGC 3256
new.summary: Ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources are bright, off-nuclear X-ray point sources, mostly associated with high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs), with a compact object accreting from a donor star at super-Eddington luminosities. Although their HMXB nature implies a connection to star formation processes, previous works have found that luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) appear to have a deficit of ULXs compared to their very high star formation rates (SFRs). Here, we analyze three Chandra observations of NGC 3256, a merging LIRG with SFR ~50-60 Msun/yr. Based on local scaling relations, it could be expected to host between 100-120 individual ULXs, which could have a non-negligible impact on the energetics and feedback processes of the galaxy. We aim to characterize all its detected X-ray point sources to determine if there is a ULX deficit in this galaxy. We also aim to explore the potential impact of host-galaxy obscuration and metallicity in said deficit. We characterize the luminosity of each X-ray point source in each Chandra observation, and use all observations to determine their potential ULX nature and the fraction of transient ULXs, as well as construct a ULX luminosity function for this galaxy. We find that the galaxy hosts 10-15 ULXs, making it one of the most ULX-rich galaxies known to date. While comparison with the ULX/SFR ratio of nearby galaxies predicted as many as ~100 ULXs, we show that, when accounting for its very high metallicity, NGC 3256 does not have a ULX deficit; and may even present an excess. While the high obscuration in LIRGs has previously been invoked to explain the ULX deficit, we conclude that it is not required to explain the ULX to SFR ratio in NGC 3256. If obscuration still plays a role, then LIRGs may actually be significantly more efficient at producing ULXs than normal galaxies (of the same metallicity), in disagreement with previous results.

new.title: Neutral hydrogen in the Shapley Supercluster core II. Gas content and star formation in the filaments connecting the core
new.summary: We investigate the neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) content of galaxies across the Shapley Supercluster (SSC) at z = 0.048 by combining new deep MeerKAT L band observations of five filament pointings with archival MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey observations of the supercluster core. Together with optical data from the Shapley Supercluster Survey, these observations provide a homogeneous view of galaxy evolution from the virialised cluster environment to the surrounding filaments. We compare the HI content, star formation activity, gas depletion timescales, and morphological properties of galaxies relative to the gas fraction and star forming main sequences. The global HI detection fraction increases from 30 per cent in the cluster centre to 45 per cent in the filaments. While HI detected galaxies in the cluster centre are dominated by transition zone systems, the filament population is shared nearly equally between star forming main sequence and transition zone detections, indicating ongoing environmental transformation. Their gas properties also differ: cluster galaxies exhibit progressively depleted HI reservoirs towards the red sequence, whereas filament galaxies remain primarily gas rich. Within the filaments, long HI depletion timescales exceeding the Hubble time are concentrated in specific populations, notably 71 per cent of transition zone and 57 per cent of gas rich detections, indicating the inefficient conversion of atomic gas into stars. The HI detected filament population is dominated by late type galaxies, while the underlying non detected population is primarily composed of early type systems, consistent with environmental pre processing before cluster infall.

new.title: Gamma-Ray Bursts from Primordial Black Hole-Induced Neutron Star Collapse
new.summary: We show that the capture and subsequent endoparasitic consumption of a neutron star (NS) by a primordial black hole (PBH) can produce a short gamma-ray burst (GRB) without forming an accretion disk. During PBH-induced NS consumption, the NS spin is amplified through angular-momentum conservation and transfer from infalling matter, while flux freezing and a differential-rotation-driven dynamo amplify the magnetic field. We find that, for rapidly rotating millisecond pulsars (MSPs), these mechanisms can power short GRBs through magnetic dipole radiation and magnetic energy release. If asteroid-mass PBHs in the range $10^{-14}M_\odot$--$10^{-11}M_\odot$ constitute the dark matter, we estimate that searches of the Fermi-GBM archive and a future MeV gamma-ray mission such as COSI could detect these bursts. We also discuss possible multimessenger counterparts, including fast radio bursts powered by magnetic energy release, kilonovae and $511\,{\rm keV}$ line emission associated with centrifugally ejected neutron-rich matter, and gravitational waves from the rapid collapse and subsequent black-hole ringdown. Together, these signals probe complementary stages of PBH-induced NS consumption.

new.title: Mauve Observations of the Eclipsing Binary System $β$ Lyrae
new.summary: We present a broadband, synoptic observing campaign of the complex eclipsing binary system $\beta$ Lyr, obtained with the first commercial astronomical satellite, Mauve, developed and operated by Blue Skies Space Ltd. Mauve's capabilities have resulted in the first multiphase monitoring of $\beta$ Lyr, covering UV and optical photometry, as well as low-resolution spectrophotometry, including the phase-folded mapping of the intensity of a number of emission lines. The different components in its spectrum vary in very different ways, indicative of a system with a number of physical components. Our data show that while most of the components show repeatable cycle-to-cycle variability, the thus far hardly observed UV emission (2000-3000 Angstrom) varies significantly from one cycle to the other, pointing to the need for simultaneous observations to understand and model the system. These observations reveal that the ultraviolet-emitting structures in this benchmark interacting binary evolve on timescales of individual orbits, challenging the assumption of a stationary accretion geometry commonly adopted in models of interacting binary stars. The quality of the data set and the fresh view that they bring to a well studied, but still poorly understood object demonstrate the scientific value of small telescopes with focused scientific capabilities, as well as the value of a new generation of commercial astronomical instrumentation.

new.title: Magnolia: a highly magnetized galaxy at redshift $z\simeq9$
new.summary: The theory of galactic magnetic field growth via dynamo action predicts that the interstellar medium (ISM) of early galaxies would remain virtually unmagnetized on large scales. However, recent observations of strong dust polarization in galaxies at redshifts $z\simeq2.6$ and $z\simeq5.6$ challenge this paradigm. If galaxies indeed host strong, large-scale, coherent magnetic fields at high-$z$, then galaxy evolution and current theories of magnetic field amplification in galaxies should be revisited. To address the full physical complexity of early magnetic field growth in galaxies, we have designed MAGNA SERRA, a suite of radiation-magneto-hydrodynamical (RMHD) cosmological zoom-in simulations with non-equilibrium chemistry. In this first paper from the MAGNA SERRA suite, we present Magnolia, a galaxy hosted in a $\simeq 10^{11}~\mathrm{M}_\odot$ dark matter halo simulated with RAMSES-RT with a $\simeq 10^4~\mathrm{M}_\odot$ mass ($\simeq 10 \,\mathrm{pc}$ spatial) resolution. We find that, at $z\simeq9$, Magnolia has a stellar mass of a few times $10^8~\mathrm{M}_\odot$ and is strongly magnetized, reaching a magnetic field of a few $\mu G$ and a plasma beta $\beta\simeq 0.1$ in the densest regions. This strong amplification occurs over a timescale of about 40~Myrs due to the highly dynamical nature of the galaxy, which creates strong compressions and shear. The power spectra of the magnetic and kinetic energies and the spectral energy transfer functions do not suggest dynamo action, but rather an initial magnetic field amplification through a large-scale compression, and a later re-organization of this field from small to large scales. Our findings show that strong galactic magnetization is possible at very high redshifts, which means that magnetic fields can play a dominant role throughout a galaxy's evolutionary history.
